hypotheses.label: Pendulum_obs experiences a real environmental or procedural oscillation (~7–14 day cycle); baseline was sampled during an atypical high phase; post-baseline drift reflects phase shift
hypotheses.rationale: Weak autocorrelation signals in pendulum data (pendulum_obs at 0.321 at 14-day lag, pendulum_lab at 0.245 at 13-day lag) hint at a ~13–14 day cyclicity or aliased 7-day pattern. If settlement environment cycles weekly (operator shift handover, thermal mass response to activity rhythm), pendulum systems could respond via vibration coupling or procedural variation. Baseline (days 1–10) spans ~1.4 cycles; post-baseline (days 11–22) could sample a different phase. However, this hypothesis faces a fatal asymmetry problem: pendulum_lab does NOT show negative drift (z = −0.40, essentially zero), while pendulum_obs does (z = −2.09). If both instruments experience the same environmental cycle, both should drift in the same direction and magnitude. The fact that one drifts and the other does not strongly argues against a shared environmental driver. Additionally, resonator instruments show no autocorrelation, consistent with electromagnetic independence from thermal/procedural cycles. This hypothesis survives only if pendulum_obs has a mechanism (e.g., mechanical looseness that amplifies environmental oscillations) that pendulum_lab lacks, but that is unparsimonious without direct evidence.

hypotheses.label: Baseline period (days 1–10) was set under atypical commissioning conditions; all instruments were systematically miscalibrated high; post-baseline readings represent true steady-state return to normal
hypotheses.rationale: Commissioning stress (cold startup, reference standards not yet verified, operator unfamiliarity) could inflate baseline calibration uniformly. If all four instruments were miscalibrated high at day 1–10, post-baseline readings would reflect a return to true steady-state at lower values, producing negative z-scores. However, this fails critically on the asymmetry test: if all four instruments were equally miscalibrated high during baseline, all four should show negative drift post-baseline. Instead, only pendulum_obs (z = −2.09) shows clear negative drift; pendulum_lab (z = −0.40), resonator_lab (z = −0.14), and resonator_obs (z = −1.25) cluster near zero or show minimal drift. Three of four instruments remain stable while one drifts, contradicting uniform commissioning miscalibration. Additionally, no visible level discontinuity at day 11 argues against sudden normalization; if commissioning error existed, a step change would be expected, not gradual drift. This hypothesis cannot explain the observed asymmetry.

hypotheses.label: All four instruments measure genuinely independent observables; baseline is sound; pendulum_obs z = −2.09 is a legitimate statistical fluctuation (false positive at ~2 SD); zero cross-correlations are expected
hypotheses.rationale: The four instruments measure independent physical quantities (pendulum period vs. resonator frequency) in separate apparatus. Zero cross-correlation across all pairs (range ±0.162–±0.454, all within chance level ±0.263–±0.296) is fully expected for independent noise. Pendulum_obs z = −2.09, while statistically significant by classical 2-sigma threshold, could be a genuine random fluctuation from the true noise distribution. Post-baseline n = 116 trials is modest; a −0.0074 beat drift against pooled SE ≈0.0035 yields z ≈ −2.1. This represents approximately a 2-tail p ≈ 0.036 false positive, within acceptable false-positive rate if this were the only hypothesis test performed. However, this explanation is increasingly implausible given (1) the asymmetry with pendulum_lab, which has comparable statistical power but shows z = −0.40, and (2) today's continued low readings (trials 255–272) showing no recovery or oscillation back toward baseline. A statistical fluctuation would be expected to persist at baseline level going forward, not to continue drifting. This hypothesis survives only as a null hypothesis of last resort; every alternative explanation should be exhausted first.

Without physical inspection of the photodiode or optical path, this remains speculative.
